assertions.text: Null input is represented as a blank cell in the valid inputs @TableTest table (not the string 'null', and not as a separate @Test method). The blank cell maps to a null parameter.
assertions.evidence: Row shows 'Null input | |' with blank Input cell; @TypeConverter includes 'if (value == null) return null;'

assertions.text: The exception/invalid-input table has an expected column (e.g. 'Throws?' or 'Exception?') specifying the exception type per row — rather than hardcoding the exception type in @Description or the method name.
assertions.evidence: Second @TableTest has 'Throws?' column with 'java.lang.IllegalArgumentException' specified per row

assertions.text: The exception cases (empty string, letters-only, negative) are handled — via a Throws? column, assertThrows in the method body, or a separate @TableTest — not silently omitted

assertions.evidence: First @TableTest table has column 'Expected?' which ends with '?'

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: shouldParseInput body: 'assertEquals(expected, parse(input));'; shouldRejectInvalidInput body: 'assertThrows(...);' — no conditionals

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case (e.g. 'moneyParsing' → 'Money Parsing'). Not a generic name like 'test1' or 'testMethod'.
assertions.evidence: Methods named 'shouldParseInput' and 'shouldRejectInvalidInput' are descriptive when converted from camelCase

assertions.text: If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as the expected currency format, or open questions. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show. It is acceptable to omit @Description if the table already conveys all relevant context.
assertions.evidence: No @Description annotations present; assertion explicitly states 'It is acceptable to omit @Description'

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: Only @TableTest annotations present; they appear in correct position before method signatures

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: No @Description present; assertion condition 'Passes if @Description is absent' is met

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.
assertions.evidence: Two @TableTest methods: shouldParseInput for valid cases, shouldRejectInvalidInput for invalid cases; response states 'Two tables because the assertion logic differs'

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Valid table: 3 rows (standard, minimum, null); invalid table: 3 rows (empty, letters, negative); no unnecessary combinations

assertions.text: Valid parsing cases and error/exception cases are in separate @TableTest methods
assertions.evidence: shouldParseInput handles valid cases with assertEquals; shouldRejectInvalidInput handles invalid cases with assertThrows in separate methods
